cues.text: Let's close this session by looking at some additional quality standards, and then working through a practice scenario that pulls together what we have learned about testing.
We begin with three standards that are easy to mix up, because they all have the word quality or testing somewhere near them, yet they serve different purposes.
First, ISO 9001.
This standard describes the requirements for a quality management system.
Notice what that means.
It is about how an organisation manages quality as a system: its processes, its responsibilities, its controls.
It is not a description of a software product itself.
Second, ISO/IEC 25010.
This one describes software and system product quality characteristics.
So where ISO 9001 looks at the management system, ISO/IEC 25010 looks at the product, and gives you a vocabulary for the qualities a software product or system should have.
Third, ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119.
This is a family of software-testing standards.
Rather than one document, think of it as a group of related standards that all concern how software testing is done.
So, to keep them apart: ISO 9001 is about the quality management system, ISO/IEC 25010 is about product quality characteristics, and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 is about software testing.
They serve different purposes, and you should not treat them as interchangeable.
Now here is an important caution.
Adoption of these standards, or even certification against them, does not prove the absence of defects.
A certificate tells you something about how an organisation works or what it has committed to; it does not guarantee that a particular piece of software is free of faults.
Alongside the standards sits QA planning.
A quality assurance plan defines several things.
It defines the objectives: what you are trying to achieve.
It defines the test approach: how you will go about testing.
It defines the environment in which testing happens.
It defines responsibilities: who does what.
It defines entry and exit criteria: the conditions that must be met before a testing activity begins, and the conditions that must be met before it can be considered complete.
It defines the evidence you will collect to show what was done and what was found.
And it defines risk-based exceptions: the cases where, because of risk, you deliberately depart from the normal plan, and you do so openly rather than silently.
Now let us move to the practice scenario.
A new school portal passes all of its unit tests.
Everything looks green.
But the portal fails when the payment service retries a timed-out transaction.
Think about what is happening here.
A payment request is sent, it times out, and the payment service tries again.
The unit tests never exercised that situation, so they could not warn us.
What should we do?
The source gives us a layered answer, level by level.
At the integration level, tests should exercise timeout and retry behaviour, and also duplicate requests.
This is where the portal and the payment service meet, so this is where the problem can actually be provoked.
At the system level, tests should validate the end-to-end records.
In other words, after the whole flow has run, do the records across the system tell a consistent and correct story?
At the acceptance level, tests should verify the school's real workflow.
This asks whether the portal supports what the school actually does, not merely whether the technical parts behave.
Then we add a regression test.
This test asserts that there is one charge per idempotency key.
An idempotency key is an identifier attached to a request so that a repeated request with the same key is recognised as the same request, and is not charged twice.
The regression test keeps this failure from quietly returning later.
Now consider the root cause.
The source says it may be a cross-service contract problem, or a transaction design problem.
It is not necessarily unit-level arithmetic.
That is a valuable lesson: the sums inside a single component may be perfectly correct, while the agreement between services, or the way a transaction is designed, is where the defect lives.
We should say only that it may be those things; the source does not claim to know.
Finally, the principle that ties this together: test assurance is risk-based and cumulative across levels.
Risk-based means you direct your testing effort toward where failure would matter most.
Cumulative across levels means confidence is built up from unit, integration, system and acceptance testing together, with each level contributing evidence that the others cannot provide.
Passing unit tests alone, as this portal shows, is not enough.
